say.text: A 52-year-old woman has a follicular carcinoma of the thyroid. Her neck has no palpable nodes.
Predict it. Which route and sites do you expect its spread to take?

choices.label: Lymphatics first, to the central and lateral neck nodes
Through the blood, mainly to the lungs and bones
Neck nodes first, then on to the lungs and bones
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because lymph drainage is the papillary route, and it is easy to carry over to this cancer.
Ask what this tumour must do to leave the gland, and which channel that step opens.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which of the two cancers the lymph route belongs to before you trust it.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because neck nodes are the first stop for papillary cancer, so they feel like the default site.
Ask whether this tumour reaches the nodes early, or whether its route follows what it invades.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether nodes are the usual site for this cancer or only for the other one.

say.text: Think about what this tumour must break through to leave the gland, and which channel that opens.
Do not reuse the lymph route you learned for papillary cancer.
Yes. This cancer is judged by capsular and vascular invasion, so its route follows the vessels.
Here is what the tumour shows. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion on histology, not by FNAC or frozen section.
Its invading cells enter veins and travel to the lungs and bones, while spread to the lymph nodes is uncommon.
Vessel invasion is the diagnostic feature. Which mechanism explains where this cancer's spread goes?

choices.label: Cells have entered veins, which carry them to lungs and bones
Cells have entered lymph channels, which drain to the neck nodes
Cells reach the neck nodes first, then veins carry them on
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because lymph drainage is the mechanism you learned for papillary cancer, so it feels familiar.
Ask which vessel the invasion you just saw actually opens, and whether capsular invasion moves cells into lymph.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which channel the invasion in the evidence actually reaches.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because the neck is the first place cancers are taught to spread, so nodes feel like step one.
Ask whether the vein route passes through the neck nodes first, or carries cells past them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether node spread is the usual route for this cancer.

say.text: Ask what the vessel invasion gives the cell access to, and then where that route ends.
The answer: vessel invasion puts follicular cells into veins, and the blood carries them to the lungs and bones.
Papillary carcinoma uses the lymphatics instead. You will see that contrast next.
Two patients. A has a lateral neck node and a small thyroid primary. B has a pathological fracture and a thyroid nodule.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: A is papillary, with B the follicular cancer
A is follicular, with B the papillary cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because the two routes are learned as a pair, and it is easy to swap them.
Ask which of the two is diagnosed by vessel invasion, and then which route that one takes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the route against the diagnostic feature, not against memory of the pair.

say.text: Start with the patient who has the neck node, and ask which channel that cancer uses to reach it.
The answer: papillary carcinoma spreads by lymphatics to the central and lateral neck nodes. Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood to the lungs and bones.
A young woman has a firm lateral neck mass. Her surgeon labels it 'lateral aberrant thyroid'.
What is this lump most likely?

choices.label: Ectopic thyroid tissue left in the lateral neck
A nodal metastasis from a papillary carcinoma
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because 'aberrant thyroid' sounds like misplaced gland, the way a thyroglossal remnant is taught.
Ask what thyroid-type cells are doing inside a lymph node in the lateral neck, and which cancer sends them there.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the name against where the mass sits: the lateral neck is a node site.

say.text: Think about where a thyroid cancer sends its cells, and what a lymph node looks like when it holds them.
The answer: the lateral 'aberrant thyroid' is a cervical node metastasis from papillary carcinoma, and it can appear with no palpable thyroid primary.
Which of these is a differentiated thyroid cancer?

choices.label: Medullary carcinoma, arising from C cells
Anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid gland
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because C-cell cancer is a classic thyroid malignancy on exam lists, so it feels like part of the family.
Ask which cell of origin the differentiated family shares, and whether C cells are among them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word differentiated in the stem before you count a thyroid malignancy.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because anaplastic carcinoma is the most aggressive thyroid cancer, so it feels like one to count with the rest.
Ask whether it keeps the differentiated behaviour that defines the family, such as iodine handling.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether aggression decides membership, or cell type and differentiation do.

say.text: Ask which cells the differentiated thyroid cancers come from, and what keeps them differentiated.
The answer: differentiated thyroid cancer is cancer of the follicular cell that keeps differentiated function. Papillary, follicular and oncocytic carcinomas are DTC.
Medullary carcinoma comes from C cells, and anaplastic carcinoma is not a DTC.
FNAC from a firm lateral neck mass shows follicular-pattern cells with ground-glass nuclei.
What is it most likely, and what do you do next?

choices.label: Ectopic thyroid tissue, benign; excise it and follow up closely
A nodal metastasis of papillary carcinoma; look for the primary
Follicular carcinoma, since the cells form follicles here
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because 'aberrant thyroid' sounds benign and tidy, so excision feels like the safe end.
Ask what a thyroid-type cell in a lymph node tells you about its source, before you decide on surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that the label names a node, and a node holding thyroid cells needs the thyroid examined.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because the pattern is follicular, so the pattern feels like the diagnosis.
Ask which feature the call of papillary carcinoma rests on, and whether the pattern alone can settle it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether architecture or nuclei decides the papillary call.

say.text: Ask which feature decides the call for papillary carcinoma, and what that feature looks like on the slide.
The answer: papillary carcinoma is called by its nuclei, so ground-glass nuclei in a lateral node point to a nodal metastasis.
Look for the thyroid primary, and do not excise it as ectopic gland.
